extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (attorneys/agents)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for examining asserted utility (especially therapeutic/pharmacological) and for determining proper inventorship in U.S. patent applications. Covers evidentiary standards, types of acceptable evidence, factors for evaluating biological data, and rules for naming and identifying inventors and joint inventorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of proof for asserted utility
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant need not prove an asserted utility 'beyond a reasonable doubt' or to statistical certainty; evidence is sufficient if, considered as a whole, it leads a person of ordinary skill in the art to conclude that the asserted utility is more likely than not true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not demand beyond-reasonable-doubt or statistical-certainty proof (In re Irons; Nelson v. Bowler). Evaluate the totality of the evidence; if a skilled person would find the asserted utility credible (preponderance standard), that suffices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character and amount of evidence varies with claim and alleged incredibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The character and amount of evidence needed to support an asserted utility will vary depending on what is claimed and whether the asserted utility appears to contravene established principles and beliefs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess utility requirements in light of the claim scope and whether the asserted use appears 'incredible' in view of current scientific understanding (Ex parte Ferguson; In re Gazave; In re Chilowsky). More extraordinary claims may require more persuasive support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special care for therapeutic or pharmacological utility assertions
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel should be particularly careful in reviewing evidence for asserted therapeutic or pharmacological utilities because courts have reversed USPTO rejections when an applicant reasonably supports such a utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give careful, substantive consideration to the evidence presented for therapeutic uses; be mindful of case law reversing rejections where reasonable support existed (Cross v. Iizuka; In re Jolles; Nelson v. Bowler).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable correlation requirement between biological activity and asserted therapeutic use
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of pharmacological or biological activity is relevant if there is a reasonable correlation between that activity and the asserted therapeutic utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants may establish reasonable correlation via statistically relevant data, sound arguments/reasoning, documentary evidence (e.g., scientific articles), or combinations thereof. Do not require proof of correlation to statistical certainty (Nelson v. Bowler).

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of acceptable evidence to support therapeutic utility
rubrics_metrics.description: Acceptable evidence includes statistically relevant experimental data, reasoned arguments, documentary evidence such as scientific articles, or any combination of these.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider all forms of evidence provided; a mix of experimental data plus a reasoned explanatory rationale can establish reasonable predictivity. Cite relevant case examples where such evidence sufficed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural similarity to known compounds can support asserted therapeutic utility
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of structural similarity to a compound known to have a particular therapeutic or pharmacological utility can support an assertion of utility for a new compound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate both the existence of structural relationship and the applicant/declarant's reasoning explaining why the structural similarity is relevant (In re Jolles). Structural similarity should be weighed along with activity data (e.g., animal screening results).

rubrics_metrics.name: In vitro and animal testing generally sufficient to support therapeutic utility
rubrics_metrics.description: Data from in vitro assays or animal models, if reasonably correlated to the asserted therapeutic utility, almost invariably will be sufficient to establish therapeutic or pharmacological utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When such data and an explanation are provided, determine whether a person skilled in the art would view them as reasonably predictive of the asserted utility (Ex parte Maas; Ex parte Balzarini). Consider factors such as test parameters, choice of animal model, relationship of measured activity to the disorder, compound characteristics, and the applicant's explanatory reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data need not come from an art-recognized animal model
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence does not have to be from an industry-accepted or art-recognized animal model for the particular disease to be relevant to the asserted utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absence of certification that a test is an industry-accepted model is not dispositive. If one skilled in the art would accept the animal tests as reasonably predictive of human utility, such evidence should be considered sufficient (In re Hartop; In re Krimmel; Ex parte Krepelka).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation factors for biological data supporting utility
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office must evaluate factors that might influence a skilled person's conclusions about whether provided data are reasonably predictive of the asserted utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifically consider test parameters, choice of animal, relationship of activity to the particular disorder, characteristics of the compound or composition, relative significance of the data provided, and, most importantly, the applicant's explanation of why the information supports the asserted utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human clinical data not required to establish utility
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no decisional law requiring an applicant to provide human clinical trial data to establish utility for inventions related to treatment of human disorders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not impose unnecessary burdens by demanding human clinical data (In re Isaacs; In re Langer; Ex parte Balzarini). If the applicant has initiated human clinical trials, presume the subject matter of that trial is reasonably predictive of the asserted therapeutic utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safety and efficacy (FDA) considerations are outside patentability review
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office must confine its review to patent law statutory requirements and should not request evidence of safety in humans or the degree of effectiveness; other agencies (e.g., FDA) handle those matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be extremely hesitant to challenge an asserted utility if experts (e.g., FDA) have assessed and found the rationale satisfactory; FDA approval is not a prerequisite for patentability, but FDA review of a use disclosed in the specification weighs heavily (In re Brana; Scott v. Finney).

rubrics_metrics.name: Credibility varies with type of claimed therapeutic effect (symptom treatment vs cure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims to treat or cure diseases with no prior cures warrant careful review; assertions of usefulness for treating symptoms may require modest evidence, while assertions of 'curing' a disease may require significantly greater evidentiary support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess credibility in light of state of the art at the time of invention; consider expert affidavits with sound reasoning as often sufficient to establish a reasonable expectation of success for challenging disease conditions (In re Sichert; In re Jolles; Ex parte Ferguson).

rubrics_metrics.name: Naming inventors and oath/declaration requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: An application must identify the inventor(s); the inventor(s) must execute the appropriate oath or declaration unless otherwise provided, with requirements depending on filing date (post- or pre-September 16, 2012 filings have different procedural rules).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow MPEP § 602.01 for detailed requirements. Foreign applicants may misunderstand U.S. naming rules; correction of inventorship may require a request under 37 CFR 1.48. If inventorship is incorrect and uncontroverted, a rejection may be appropriate (see MPEP § 2157, § 2137).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventor must contribute to conception
rubrics_metrics.description: To be an inventor, a person must contribute to the conception of the invention; contribution to conception is the threshold question in determining inventorship, and merely suggesting a desired result (without means) does not make one an inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduction to practice is generally irrelevant to inventorship except in rare simultaneous-conception-and-reduction situations (Fiers v. Revel). For chemical compounds, conception must be of the specific claimed compounds (Board of Education v. American Bioscience; Ex parte Smernoff). See MPEP § 2138.04–.05 for evidence required to establish conception or reduction to practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventor need not personally reduce the invention to practice
rubrics_metrics.description: An inventor is not required to reduce the invention to practice personally; implementation by others following directions does not necessarily negate inventorship when inventive skill wasn't required for the implementation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technicians following instructions are typically not inventors (Mattor v. Coolegem); those who implement steps without inventive skill do not preclude the conceiver from being an inventor. Reduction to practice done on an inventor's behalf counts (In re DeBaun; Fritsch v. Lin).

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint inventorship standards (35 U.S.C. 116)
rubrics_metrics.description: When an invention is made by two or more persons jointly, they shall apply for patent jointly. Joint inventors need not have worked together physically, need not have made the same type or amount of contribution, and need not contribute to every claim — contribution to at least one claim suffices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There must be some quantum of collaboration or connection (e.g., collaboration, common direction, one inventor building on another’s report) — mere complete lack of contact is insufficient (Kimberly-Clark v. Procter & Gamble). Partial contributions that are original and significant qualify. Contribution to a means-plus-function element can make one a joint inventor as to that claim (Ethicon Inc. v. United States Surgical). See MPEP § 2109.01 and § 602.09 for correction procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventorship 'by another' and differing inventive entities
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventorship is 'by another' when there are different inventive entities and at least one inventor is not in common between the applications; special practice applies for first-to-file (AIA) versus pre-AIA cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow MPEP § 2153.01(a) for FITF (AIA) cases and MPEP § 2136.04 for pre-AIA cases. Determine whether inventive entities differ and whether an inventor is in common when assessing issues like derivation or benefit claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuing application benefit under 35 U.S.C. 120 requires a common inventor and proper disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: An application claiming benefit under 35 U.S.C. 120 must name at least one inventor named in the earlier application, and the earlier application must disclose the named inventor’s invention in at least one claim in the manner provided by 35 U.S.C. 112 (for post-September 16, 2012 filings) or the first paragraph (for pre-September 16, 2012 filings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: So long as at least one inventor is common and other statutory requirements are met, the Office permits the 120 benefit claim without additional notifications. The examiner must also examine the earlier application to confirm a common inventor and compliance with 35 U.S.C. 120 and 37 CFR 1.78; benefit may be permitted without full examination of the earlier app unless intervening references make it necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventors must be natural persons
rubrics_metrics.description: An inventor or joint inventors named on a patent or patent application must be natural persons (human beings); corporations, sovereigns, or non-human entities cannot be inventors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow statutory definitions (35 U.S.C. 100(f), 100(g)) and case law (Thaler v. Vidal; Univ. of Utah v. Max-Planck-Gesellschaft). Ensure inventor listings identify natural persons; do not accept non-human entities as inventors.
